extracted.intended_audience: general reading public interested in the Maria Monk exposé; Protestant critics and supporters evaluating the truth of the 'Awful Disclosures'
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the credibility and truth of a first‑person exposé/pamphlet based on witness testimony, affidavits, physical evidence, and the responses (or silence) of accused institutions. Focus is on what counts as convincing proof and reliable corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening/inspection of the Hotel Dieu Nunnery
rubrics_metrics.description: The decisive test of the book's truth is the physical opening and inspection of the Hotel Dieu Nunnery at Montreal: 'Then, sir, and not till then, will the great question be settled,--Is our book true or false?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand that the accused institution allow inspection; publicize the invitation and make inspection the primary arbiter of truth. The text proposes that an on‑site inspection is more conclusive than affidavits or public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial public investigation with agreed composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose an investigation 'before an impartial assembly, over which shall preside seven gentlemen; three to be selected by the Roman Priests, three by the Executive Committee ... and the Seventh as Chairman, to be chosen by the six.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define an investigative procedure that balances representation from both parties and appoints a neutral chair; set venue, decorum, and rules in advance so findings are accepted as fair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration from multiple, independent witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: The book's statements are supported by 'confirmation from various sources' and by 'two important witnesses spontaneously appeared' — multiple independent witnesses strengthen credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer testimony that arises spontaneously and independently in different places (e.g., Montreal and New York). Certificates listing several subscribers willing to answer reasonable inquiries increase weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sworn affidavits and proper authentication
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits sworn before a commissioner (e.g., 'Sworn before me ... Commissioner of Deeds') are presented as formal evidence of events and acquaintance with the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that affidavits carry dates, signatures, and notarization; such formalities increase evidentiary weight. Note who administered the oath and where it was taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific, verifiable descriptive details
rubrics_metrics.description: Credible testimony includes concrete, checkable details (processions at three P.M., dress of novices, mention of belts and gags, underground passages located on specific streets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give and seek particulars—times, places, physical objects, routines—that can be independently verified (by inspection, other records, or credible witnesses). Vague or general claims are weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ocular demonstration / physical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Firsthand physical observation of features (e.g., subterranean passages found during pipe‑laying; removed flat stones revealing passages) is offered as strong support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value physical or material proof observed by witnesses; note attempts by accused parties to prevent further examination (which the text treats as suspicious).

rubrics_metrics.name: Named witnesses vs. anonymous 'delicacy'
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirmation that witnesses of 'known character and unimpeachable veracity' are preferable to unnamed 'lady's delicacy'; withholding names for delicacy reduces the weight of testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer testimony with names and contactability. Anonymous or unnamed sources require extra corroboration; the use of 'delicacy' as an excuse is criticized in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of neutral third parties and witness bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether testimonies were given in private or with neutral observers, and whether witnesses are inimical or friendly to the claimant (e.g., 'those who are named are most of them inimical to me').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess potential bias or hostility of witnesses and the presence/absence of neutral third parties when judging reliability. Hostile witnesses may undercut credibility of their statements; neutral corroboration strengthens it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context of interviews (emotional state and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews occurred 'on two of the most distressing days of my life'; the claimant argues that statements made under such conditions might be misunderstood or misreported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the emotional and situational context in which witnesses spoke: distress, fatigue, or shock can affect recall and interpretation. Cross‑check statements made in calm settings where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic and institutional breadth of corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence and witnesses appearing in multiple cities (Montreal, New York, Boston, etc.) and institutions (hospitals, schools) are used to argue for wider corroboration of claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give added weight to corroboration that spans jurisdictions and independent institutions rather than confined to a single sympathetic locale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to litigate or prosecute as evidentiary signal
rubrics_metrics.description: The text challenges priests to 'institute a criminal process against her, or a civil suit against the publishers' and treats their failure to do so as suggestive of inability to disprove the charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret unwillingness to pursue legal remedies or public formal challenges as a potential indicator of weakness in the accused party's defense—but distinguish strategic non‑litigation from inability to defend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence or failure to publicly rebut
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative treats the priests' and nuns' failure to 'come out' or publicly deny accusations as significant: 'Our longings meet only with disappointment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider prolonged public silence or absence from offered forums as at least politically damaging; however, silence must be weighed against possible tactical or legal reasons for non‑response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical relevance and quality of counter‑affidavits
rubrics_metrics.description: Counter‑affidavits must directly address core factual claims; the text criticizes disjointed or irrelevant refutations (e.g., the New York Catholic Diary's mockery of Mr. Miller's affidavit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize counter‑evidence for logical soundness and direct relevance. Fallacious or tangential rebuttals do not meaningfully undercut central claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common notary or affidavit origin as a possible coordination signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that one commissioner (Dr. Robertson) gave or took multiple of the affidavits, which raises the question of coordination or dependence among statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note patterns in how affidavits were obtained (same notary, same dates); closely similar provenance among many affidavits may indicate coordination and should affect weighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of institutional behavior and treatment as indirect evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of how the claimant was treated in hospitals and by nurses/priests (attempts to isolate, pressure to return to clergy) are used to infer the existence of the institutional practices complained of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat consistent behavioral patterns toward the claimant (isolation, discouraging conversion, restricted communication) as circumstantial support for allegations about institutional character, while seeking corroboration.
